# Instructions

This week, you learned several more functions from the dplyr package (pronounced DEE-ply-er). These functions help you work with the rows and columns in your data set.

You'll use these skills to add a new column that contains the cumulative financial IHP assistance awarded over time for the disasters in New York for which the IHP was declared.

To learn more about the variables contained in the data set, refer to the data dictionary: https://rstudio.github.io/academy-tidyverse-fema/assets/disasters_dictionary.html

## Create and select columns

In this milestone, you'll create a new variable that contains the cumulative value of `total_ihp_awarded` over time for the IHP-declared disasters in New York. You'll then select the columns that tell that story.

### Part 2 - Create

Run the code below to see a table.

```{r}
#| label: recreate-this
#| message: false
solution <- readr::read_csv("data/milestone03.csv")
solution
```

Your task is to use what you've learned about the dplyr package to transform `disasters` into this table. You will need to:

1. Filter the data to records from New York (`state` is `"NY"`) where the IHP was declared (`ih_program_declared` is `1`)
2. Remove the records that have no award data (`total_ihp_awarded` is `NA`). *Hint:* once `cumsum()` meets a missing value, every value from there on is `NA`.
3. Arrange the rows by `declaration_date`, from earliest to latest. Many records share a declaration date (every designated area of a declaration does); keep those in their original order, which is what `arrange()` does when you sort by `declaration_date` alone.
4. Create a new column named `cumul_total_ihp_awarded`, which contains the result of `cumsum()` applied to `total_ihp_awarded`
5. Select six columns: `fema_declaration_string`, `declaration_date`, `incident_type`, `designated_area`, `total_ihp_awarded`, `cumul_total_ihp_awarded`

Work in the code chunk below. Save the result as `ny_ihp_cumul`.

```{r}

```

Run the following code chunk to test whether you have the same answer as the solution:

```{r}
#| label: compare
#| eval: false
waldo::compare(ny_ihp_cumul, solution, tolerance = 1e-4)
```

Look at how `cumul_total_ihp_awarded` grows from row to row. Which declarations added the most?
